Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

vignette: The night her cousin pulled her into the dim hallway of the family hall, the music swelling outside with laughter, Tiana felt the ground dissolve beneath her. What had begun as a familiar gathering quickly curdled when his hand gripped her wrist and his weight pinned her against the peeling wallpaper. Now, simply being near relatives who resemble him sends a cold jolt through her chest. When a neighbor laughs too freely at a community potluck, or when the quiet comfort of a sunlit kitchen makes her shoulders drop even an inch, her nervous system instantly wires that ease to the old violation. The feeling of relaxation forces the memory of that hallway back into her mind, unbidden and relentless. The mere sight of a familiar relative or a sudden sense of discomfort triggers a surge of dread that locks her throat tight and keeps her body on constant alert. Because those cues arrive without warning, she immediately reaches for her heavy makeup or excuses herself to the doorway to escape the rising panic. Walking through parish halls and visiting parishioners for her social ministry work, Tiana finds herself scanning the back corners of meeting rooms and instinctively angling her chair toward the door. She is convinced she is no longer capable of the compassion that defined her, and she is certain there is a fundamental defect in her character that makes her unclean. That belief in her own brokenness dictates her daily armor, forcing her to eat excessively whenever her shame becomes heavy and ensuring she always stays near the exit in every meeting. Because she views herself as fundamentally unsafe, those very appraisals keep her hyperalert to potential danger, turning every glance into a threat assessment. The constant conviction that she is irreparably damaged also sharpens her eyes to spot the slightest shift in a room’s energy, ensuring that neutral interactions quickly become loaded with fear. Over the months, the cognitive architecture of her fear tightened into a self-sustaining trap. The uncontrolled replay of the assault—vivid and clear, playing like a reel of film in her head—directly fuels her physical tension. As the intrusive images flood her mind, her muscles coil and her breath shortens, pushing her body into a state of constant readiness to react. She responds to that rising physiological alarm by retreating to the doorframe or doubling down on a second helping of dinner, which in turn keeps the traumatic script looping in her memory. The face-sealing makeup and the compulsive overeating do not quiet the past; instead, they ensure the memories return sharper and more frequently. By hiding behind her mask and numbing herself with food, she inadvertently sustains her physiological alarm, guaranteeing that her threat system remains permanently engaged. Her threat system never learned to stand down. The hyper-vigilance and the compulsion to repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked drain her strength, leaving her exhausted and irritable with her husband. When the compulsion to check locks overtakes her, she doubles down on the exit-seeking and overeating to manage the mounting panic. This relentless physiological storm loops back to amplify her triggers, meaning that a casual touch or a relaxed sigh now instantly signals danger and forces another intrusive memory. Because she stays near exits and forces herself to consume food to numb the panic, she inadvertently trains her brain to associate safety-seeking with the original violation, which rapidly escalates her triggers. She came to therapy last Tuesday because the exhaustion finally outweighed the fear of being exposed. She is terrified that her husband will eventually see the real her, but she desperately hopes that someone might help her untangle the knot before the past completely erases the woman she used to be.
